name: Vatican City
summary: The smallest country in the world, created in 1929 by the Lateran Treaty between Italy and the Pope after the Papal States were lost in 1870; seat of the Catholic Church.

location.value: The smallest sovereign state by area and population: 0.49 km² in the infobox (195th) but 44 hectares in the text, so the area figures differ slightly.

terrain.value: Part of the Vatican Hill, enclosed by walls, with gardens and St Peter’s Square.

climate.value: Mediterranean: hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters.

resources.value: No natural resources; income comes from donations, museum tickets and investments.

disasters.value: Few natural disasters; floods and earthquakes affect the wider Rome area.

urbanisation.value: Entirely urban: palaces, offices, St Peter’s Basilica and gardens.

disease.value: Residents use modern health care, much of it in Rome.

migration.value: Almost all residents come from other countries to work there, and citizenship usually ends when the job ends.

economicBase.value: Funded by sales of stamps, coins, medals and tourist mementos, museum admission fees and publications. Peter’s Pence is a separate Holy See fund. The state had a surplus of €6.7 million in 2007 and a deficit of over €15 million in 2008.

tradeRoutes.value: Customs union with its larger neighbour.

wealth.value: Funded by the worldwide Catholic Church; its exact finances have often been criticised as unclear.

moneyAndTax.value: The euro, under an agreement with the EU; the Vatican issues its own euro coins.

inequality.value: Residents are mostly clergy and staff with housing provided; there is no large poor population.

governmentType.value: The Holy See, which has permanent observer status at the UN, is distinct from Vatican City State.

keyRulers.value: Pius XI (the Lateran Treaty was signed on 11 February 1929 and took effect on 7 June 1929); Francis; Leo XIV (Robert Francis Prevost, elected 8 May 2025). John Paul II is not covered in the part read.

succession.value: Popes elected by cardinals in a conclave.

institutions.value: The Pope, the Roman Curia (the Church’s government), the Governorate of the city, and the Vatican Bank.

stability.value: Very stable: power passes by election of a new pope.

eliteConflict.value: Reports of factions and financial scandals in the Curia; their extent is debated.

armyAndTech.value: The Pontifical Swiss Guard was founded by Pope Julius II on 22 January 1506.

majorWars.value: Neutral in the Second World War, though surrounded by Fascist Italy.

territoryChange.value: No territorial change since the Lateran Treaty of 1929.

alliancesRivals.value: The Holy See has diplomatic relations with most countries of the world.

inventions.value: No inventions; Vatican Radio (1931) was set up with Guglielmo Marconi’s help.

scienceEducation.value: Pius XI founded the Pontifical Academy of Sciences in 1936; the Vatican Observatory’s origins date to the 16th century.

openness.value: Open borders with Italy; millions of visitors come every year.

communicationTransport.value: Uses Rome’s roads; has its own tiny railway station, helipad and post office.

religion.value: Catholicism is the state religion; all citizens, residents and places of worship in the city are Catholic.

languageWriting.value: Italian is the working language; Latin is used for official Church documents.

artsArchitecture.value: St Peter’s Basilica, the Sistine Chapel (Michelangelo) and the Raphael Rooms; the Vatican Museums.

socialStructure.value: Cardinals and clergy, the Swiss Guard (since 1506), lay staff and their families.

sharedIdentity.value: Identity as the centre of the worldwide Catholic Church rather than as a nation.

dailyLife.value: Most of its thousands of workers live in Rome and commute in each day.

ideasReligions.value: Catholic teaching for over a billion Catholics; the Second Vatican Council (1962–65) reformed Church practice.

colonisation.value: Successor to the Papal States, which Italy took over in 1870.

riseSignals.value: The Lateran Treaty was signed on 11 February 1929 and took effect on 7 June 1929, creating the modern city-state.

peakPeriod.value: Its world influence grew after the Second Vatican Council and with travelling popes such as John Paul II.

declineSignals.value: Abuse scandals and falling church attendance in Europe have hurt the Church’s reputation.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
